title: Lab Safety: Same Shield, Right Rule, Alarm First
summary: See why every specimen gets the same protection, which OSHA rule covers germs versus chemicals, and the order of actions when a fire starts.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 1 Hit 10 (Standard Precautions), Hit 15 (RACE order; PASS added from OSHA) and Trap 6 (bloodborne-pathogens vs chemical rules). Hit 14 (GHS/SDS) is only partly taught — the SDS ingredient-threshold statement was not verified — so it is not counted. Adds that OSHA 1910.1030 still uses “universal precautions” wording and that HazCom was updated in 2024.

objectives: State the principle and scope of Standard Precautions, including the sweat exception.
Explain how Standard Precautions relate to Universal Precautions and Body Substance Isolation.
Match infectious versus chemical hazards to the correct OSHA standard.
Give the alarm-first fire response and the PASS extinguisher steps.

scenes.title: Skip the gloves for a “clean” patient?
scenes.altText: Two blood tubes sit side by side: one labelled with a known HIV infection, the other labelled “no known infections”. A new trainee reaches for the second tube without gloves and asks whether gloves are needed. The two tubes then look identical, with a question mark.

cues.text: Two tubes arrive. One patient has a known HIV infection. The other has no known infections at all.
A new trainee asks: “Do I really need gloves for the second one?”
Look closer. From the outside the two tubes are identical — and an infection that has never been diagnosed is invisible.

props.text: Do I really need gloves for this one?

scenes.title: Standard Precautions: one shield for every sample
scenes.altText: A row of materials — blood, body fluids, secretions, excretions, non-intact skin and mucous membranes — each gets a shield icon; sweat is the one item set aside. Every patient’s specimen gets the same shield. Then a short history: Universal Precautions plus Body Substance Isolation merge into Standard Precautions (CDC, 1996). Finally, protective-equipment icons and hand hygiene appear around a person.

cues.text: The answer is Standard Precautions: treat every patient’s blood and body fluids as if they could carry an infection — whatever the label says.
That covers blood, body fluids, secretions and excretions — except sweat — plus non-intact skin and mucous membranes.
Because we can’t see who is infected, we protect against everyone the same way. That removes guesswork.
Standard Precautions were first recommended by CDC in 1996. They combined two older ideas: Universal Precautions and Body Substance Isolation.
At the bench, that means barriers — gloves, lab coat or gown, and eye or face protection when splashes are possible — plus hand hygiene.
It also means safe handling of sharps. The point is simple: the same protection, for every sample, every time.

scenes.title: Two hazards, two different OSHA rules
scenes.altText: Two columns. Left: a needle and a blood tube point to a document labelled “Bloodborne Pathogens standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030 (published 1991)”. Right: an acid bottle points to two documents: “Laboratory standard, 29 CFR 1910.1450 (1990)” and “Hazard Communication, 29 CFR 1910.1200 — aligned with GHS in 2012; Safety Data Sheets replace MSDS”. An SDS sheet with an “English” tag appears.

cues.text: Labs face two very different kinds of hazard: infectious material, and hazardous chemicals. OSHA handles them with different rules.
Infectious exposure — blood, needlesticks — falls under the Bloodborne Pathogens standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030, published in 1991.
Chemicals fall under other rules: the Laboratory standard, 1910.1450 from 1990, which requires a chemical hygiene plan, and the Hazard Communication standard, 1910.1200.
In 2012, Hazard Communication was aligned with the global system called GHS. The old Material Safety Data Sheets became Safety Data Sheets, which must be in English.
Interesting wrinkle: OSHA’s bloodborne rule still uses the older phrase “universal precautions,” even though CDC’s term is now Standard Precautions.

scenes.title: If there’s a fire
scenes.altText: A small fire icon appears in a wastebasket. Four steps light up in order: rescue anyone in immediate danger, raise the alarm, confine the fire by closing doors, then extinguish only if it is small and your exit is clear — otherwise evacuate. A fire-extinguisher sequence follows: Pull the pin, Aim at the base, Squeeze the handle, Sweep side to side.

cues.text: A small fire starts in a wastebasket. The common hospital order is often taught as RACE.
Rescue anyone in immediate danger. Raise the alarm — call for help before you fight. Confine the fire by closing doors.
Only then extinguish, and only if the fire is small and your escape route stays clear behind you. If in doubt, evacuate.
To use an extinguisher, OSHA teaches PASS: Pull the pin. Aim low, at the base of the fire. Squeeze the handle. Sweep side to side.
If the extinguisher empties and the fire is still burning, or the fire grows, leave immediately.

props.label: E — Extinguish if small, exit clear

scenes.title: Pairs the exam likes to blur
scenes.altText: Two comparison cards: Standard Precautions (CDC 1996; all patients; blood, body fluids, secretions, excretions except sweat, non-intact skin, mucous membranes) versus Universal Precautions (the older approach, still the term in OSHA’s bloodborne rule). Then OSHA 1910.1030 bloodborne pathogens (infectious exposure) versus 1910.1450 and 1910.1200 (chemicals, chemical hygiene plan, labels and SDS).

cues.text: Exam pair one: Standard Precautions versus Universal Precautions.
Standard Precautions came from CDC in 1996 and combine Universal Precautions with Body Substance Isolation. OSHA’s bloodborne rule still says “universal precautions.”
Exam pair two: which OSHA rule? Match the rule to the hazard.
Needlesticks and blood: 1910.1030. Chemicals: the Laboratory standard 1910.1450 and Hazard Communication 1910.1200, with labels and Safety Data Sheets.

scenes.title: Same shield · People, Phone, Door, Douse
scenes.altText: Memory aid: one shield over a row of identical tubes (“same shield, every sample”). Then four picture steps: a person (rescue), a phone/alarm (alarm), a closed door (confine), and a spray (extinguish). A card lists where the aid breaks down.

cues.text: Memory aid one: same shield, every sample. No patient gets less protection because their label looks “clean.”
Memory aid two, for fire: People, Phone, Door, Douse — rescue people, raise the alarm, shut the door, then douse it if it’s small.
Where it breaks: your facility’s fire plan may order steps differently, and “douse” is optional — if the fire isn’t small or your exit isn’t clear, evacuate instead.

props.text: Same shield · People → Phone → Door → Douse

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: Follow your facility’s fire plan · douse only if small and exit clear — otherwise evacuate

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: A shield over identical specimen tubes, next to two OSHA rule documents labelled “germs” and “chemicals”, and a small fire with an alarm-first arrow.

cues.text: Protect yourself from every sample the same way with Standard Precautions, match the hazard to its OSHA rule — 1910.1030 for blood and needles, 1910.1450 and 1910.1200 for chemicals — and raise the alarm before you ever fight a fire.

explanation.what: Plain language: you can’t tell from a tube who is infected, so you protect yourself from every sample the same way. Scientific terms: Standard Precautions — treating blood, body fluids, secretions and excretions (except sweat), non-intact skin and mucous membranes of all patients as potentially infectious. Chemical hazards are handled separately, by chemical-safety rules, labels and Safety Data Sheets.
explanation.why: Many infections are undiagnosed, so precautions based only on known diagnoses leave gaps. Standard Precautions, first recommended by CDC in 1996, combined the older Universal Precautions with Body Substance Isolation so that protection doesn’t depend on a label. Infectious and chemical hazards injure in different ways, which is why OSHA regulates them under different standards.
explanation.measure: This is a safety-practice concept: what a lab “observes” is whether the right controls are in place — barriers (gloves, gown, eye/face protection) and hand hygiene for every specimen, safe sharps handling, an exposure control program under OSHA 1910.1030, a chemical hygiene plan under 1910.1450, labels and Safety Data Sheets under 1910.1200, and a fire plan in which the alarm is raised before anyone fights a fire.
explanation.differs: Standard Precautions (CDC term since 1996) vs Universal Precautions (the older approach; still the wording in OSHA 1910.1030). OSHA 1910.1030 covers occupational exposure to blood and other potentially infectious materials; 1910.1450 (the Laboratory standard, 1990) and 1910.1200 (Hazard Communication; GHS-aligned in 2012, updated 2024) cover hazardous chemicals. RACE describes the order of actions in a fire; PASS describes how to use an extinguisher.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: “which patients do Standard Precautions apply to?” (all), the sweat exception, which OSHA standard addresses needlesticks versus chemicals, what replaced the MSDS (the SDS), and fire-response order (alarm before extinguishing; PASS steps). A common trap pairs the bloodborne-pathogens rule with chemical hazards because both are OSHA.

comparisons.title: Standard Precautions vs Universal Precautions

left.label: Standard Precautions
points: Blood, body fluids, secretions, excretions (except sweat), non-intact skin, mucous membranes
Combines Universal Precautions and Body Substance Isolation

right.label: Universal Precautions
points: Older CDC approach focused on bloodborne pathogens
Still the term used in OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030

comparisons.distinguisher: Standard Precautions extend protection to excretions and secretions (except sweat) for every patient; “universal precautions” is the older term that OSHA’s rule kept.

comparisons.title: Which OSHA rule?

left.label: 29 CFR 1910.1030 Bloodborne Pathogens
points: Blood and other potentially infectious materials

comparisons.distinguisher: The hazard decides the rule: infectious material → 1910.1030; chemicals → 1910.1450 and 1910.1200.

mnemonic.text: Same shield, every sample — and for fire: People, Phone, Door, Douse.
mnemonic.explanation: Every specimen gets the same protection, regardless of the label. In a fire: rescue People, raise the alarm (Phone), confine by closing the Door, then Douse only if it is small and your exit is clear.
mnemonic.limitation: Facilities write their own fire plans and may order or name steps differently. “Douse” is conditional — if the fire is beyond its earliest stage or your exit is threatened, evacuate. Standard Precautions are the baseline; some infections also need transmission-based precautions, which this aid does not cover.

analogyLimitations: Icons for PPE, alarms and doors are cartoons; real PPE choice depends on the task and the risk of splash or spray.
Tubes are drawn identical to make the point that infection status can’t be seen; real labels differ.
Regulation documents are simplified cards, not the full text of the standards.
takeaway: Protect yourself from every sample the same way with Standard Precautions, match the hazard to its OSHA rule — 1910.1030 for blood and needles, 1910.1450 and 1910.1200 for chemicals — and raise the alarm before you ever fight a fire.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Standard Precautions?

options.text: Blood, body fluids, secretions and excretions (except sweat), non-intact skin and mucous membranes of ALL patients are treated as potentially infectious
options.rationale: Correct. This is CDC’s definition of the principle behind Standard Precautions, applied to every patient regardless of diagnosis.

options.text: Precautions are used only for patients with a diagnosed infection
options.rationale: Incorrect. The whole point is that undiagnosed infections are invisible, so protection is applied to every patient.

options.text: Sweat is included along with all other body fluids
options.rationale: Incorrect. Sweat is the stated exception in CDC’s definition.

options.text: They replace the need for hand hygiene when gloves are worn
options.rationale: Incorrect. Hand hygiene is a core element of Standard Precautions; gloves do not replace it.

questions.stem: A laboratory must write a chemical hygiene plan for the solvents and acids used on its benches. Which OSHA standard requires this?

options.text: 29 CFR 1910.1450, Occupational exposure to hazardous chemicals in laboratories
options.rationale: Correct. The Laboratory standard (1990) applies to laboratory use of hazardous chemicals and requires a chemical hygiene plan.
Incorrect. 1910.1030 covers occupational exposure to blood and other potentially infectious materials, not chemicals.
Incorrect. CLIA regulates laboratory testing quality and certification, not workplace chemical safety.
Incorrect. Standard Precautions are CDC infection-prevention practices, not an OSHA chemical standard.

questions.stem: A small fire starts in a laboratory wastebasket. Before attempting to use a portable extinguisher, what should a worker do?

options.text: Sound the alarm and make sure there is a clear escape route
options.rationale: Correct. OSHA advises sounding the alarm and identifying a safe evacuation path before approaching a fire; then PASS — Pull, Aim at the base, Squeeze, Sweep.

options.text: Aim the extinguisher at the top of the flames
options.rationale: Incorrect. PASS says to aim low, at the base of the fire.

options.text: Open the doors to let the smoke out
options.rationale: Incorrect. Doors are closed to confine the fire, not opened.

options.text: Keep fighting the fire even if the extinguisher empties
options.rationale: Incorrect. If the extinguisher empties or the fire grows beyond its earliest stage, evacuate immediately.

claims.text: Standard Precautions treat blood, body fluids, secretions, excretions except sweat, nonintact skin and mucous membranes as potentially infectious.
Standard Precautions were first recommended in CDC’s 1996 guideline and combine Universal Precautions and Body Substance Isolation.
OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030 applies to occupational exposure to blood or other potentially infectious materials, was published December 6, 1991, and uses the term “universal precautions.”
OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1450 (1990) applies to laboratory use of hazardous chemicals.
OSHA Hazard Communication (1910.1200) was aligned with GHS in 2012 and amended in 2024; safety data sheets must be in English.
PASS: Pull the pin, Aim at the base, Squeeze the handle, Sweep side to side; sound the alarm and identify an exit before approaching; evacuate if the extinguisher empties or the fire grows.
Standard Precautions at the bench include gloves, gown/lab coat, eye or face protection when splashes are possible, hand hygiene and safe sharps handling.
claims.note: Elements listed in the CDC guideline were not extracted verbatim in this session.

claims.text: The Laboratory standard requires a chemical hygiene plan.
claims.note: Standard content of 1910.1450; the specific paragraph was not quoted in this session.

claims.text: Fire response order commonly taught as RACE: Rescue, Alarm, Confine, Extinguish/Evacuate.
claims.note: Widely used training acronym; not found in a consulted official source (OSHA’s eTool teaches alarm-first and PASS but not RACE).

claims.text: Safety Data Sheets replaced Material Safety Data Sheets under the GHS-aligned HazCom.
claims.note: Consistent with the 2012 rule; the replacement wording was not quoted in this session.

accuracyFlags.issue: Reviewer Trap 6 dates the bloodborne-pathogens standard to 1992; the Federal Register publication is December 6, 1991 (56 FR 64175). The 1992 date likely refers to when it took effect.
Reviewer says Standard Precautions “replaced” Universal Precautions in 1996. That is CDC’s terminology; OSHA’s regulation still requires “universal precautions,” so both terms appear on exams.
OSHA rules are US-specific. Philippine occupational-safety and DOH biosafety rules are not covered.

morphology.note: A safety-practice concept; visuals are schematic.
